title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vanishing twin syndrome is a condition in which 1 fetus in a multiple gestation disappears in the uterus during early pregnancy, most often during the first trimester. The fetal tissue is typically reabsorbed by the maternal system or the surviving twin, and the mother may experience minimal or nonspecific symptoms such as vaginal bleeding or cramping. Advances in ultrasonography have increased recognition of this phenomenon, which previously went undiagnosed before the advent of early prenatal imaging. Risk factors include assisted reproductive technology, advanced maternal age, and multifetal gestations. Clinical implications range from negligible impact on the surviving twin to potential complications such as preterm labor, growth restriction, or emotional distress for the family. Accurate recognition of ultrasound findings and understanding genetic considerations are essential for clinicians to provide informed, compassionate, patient-centered care.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course provides clinicians with knowledge of the pathophysiology, diagnostic techniques, and management considerations related to vanishing twin syndrome. Participants learn to recognize characteristic ultrasound findings, assess risk factors, and apply evidence-based strategies for patient counseling and follow-up. The activity emphasizes effectively communicating the condition’s clinical and emotional impact to patients and families. Collaboration among obstetricians, maternal-fetal medicine specialists, radiologists, genetic counselors, and nursing staff enhances diagnostic accuracy, supports shared decision-making, and ensures continuity of prenatal care. By integrating interprofessional expertise, clinicians strengthen the quality of counseling, optimize monitoring strategies, and improve maternal–fetal outcomes, while also addressing the psychological aspects of pregnancy loss within a multiple gestation.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Vanishing twin syndrome (VTS) occurs whena fetus in a multiple pregnancy spontaneously dies and is partially or fully reabsorbed, usually in the first trimester. Some definitions require that cardiac activity be previously confirmed in all fetuses before the loss. [1] Early ultrasound detection has led to an increase in the diagnosis of this condition. Estimates suggest VTS occurs in up to 36% of twin pregnancies and 30% to 50% of higher-order multiple pregnancies. [2] The syndrome may involve monochorionic or dichorionic gestations with differing clinical implications. In dichorionic pregnancies, the impact on the surviving twin is often minimal. However, in monochorionic pregnancies, shared placental circulation can increase the risk of complications such as neurological injury or preterm birth in the surviving fetus due to vascular disturbances following the demise of 1 fetus.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The natural history of VTS usually follows a course of early fetal loss, followed by sonographic evidence of a shrinking or absent gestational sac. While many cases are asymptomatic, some individuals may experience mild cramping or vaginal bleeding. Understanding the anatomy and natural history of VTS is essential for appropriate prenatal counseling, monitoring, and interprofessional coordination of care throughout pregnancy.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Etiology
content: In the majority of cases, the exact cause of a vanishing twin remains unclear, but certain etiological or risk factors are considered to be associated with its occurrence. [3] [4] These include the following: Advanced maternal age (usually older than 35) [5] Chromosomal abnormalities in the deceased twin Use of assisted reproductive techniques, such as in vitro fertilization, especially when transferring multiple embryos [6] Anatomical abnormalities of the placenta Genetic and teratogenic factors [7]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Before the advent of ultrasound, little was known about the phenomenon of VTS. In 1945, Stoeckel discovered that the rate of multiple gestations is greater than the rate of their births. That is to say, a twin or even multiple fetuses can be lost during a multifetal pregnancy before the mother is even aware of the loss or the fact that she was carrying multiple fetuses. [8] Since the widespread use of ultrasonography in early pregnancy, VTS has been more frequently diagnosed. VTS is thought to happen in 15% to 36% of twin pregnancies and in 30% to 50% of pregnancies that begin with at least 3 or more gestational sacs.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Study results have shown that many of the patients who experience a vanishing twin are older than 30. [5] VTS is estimated to occur in 20% to 30% of ART pregnancies. This phenomenon is becoming increasingly prevalent with the use of assisted reproductive methods, as more than 1 embryo is transferred to the uterus; consequently, the rate of multiple gestations also increases. [4] [9] Results from a retrospective cohort study of ART twin pregnancies complicated by intrauterine hemorrhage early in pregnancy found that the pregnancies complicated by hemorrhage had a higher rate of VTS, 26.9% versus 18.7%. Similarly, intrauterine hemorrhage before visible fetal heart motion was more likely to be associated with VTS, 89.5% versus 20.1%. [10]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Abnormalities that bring about the vanishing fetus are usually present from very early development, as opposed to happening from an intense acute insult. [4] Results from a study including 30 patients performed by Robinson and Caines demonstrated the fetal surface of the placenta as an empty and flattened sac, as pathological evidence of the disappearing twin. Another study conducted by Finberg and Birnholz found a small area containing 30 mL of dark brown blood in the pathological specimen of abortion; this observation was followed by the appearance of a hemorrhagic second sac seen on ultrasonography. As per Finberg and Birnholz, if the pregnancy ends in abortion, the results are that the product of conception is commonly fragmented. On the contrary, if the pregnancy continues to term, the subsequent sac may have been removed or expelled, resorbed or fragmented, or may persevere as a small atretic section that is not noticed even after careful examination of the placenta and the membranes. [11]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Resorption: Although resorption is the most likely physiologic explanation for the vanishing of the specific proportion of the gestational sac, the incidence of resorption is still unknown. Different study results show that resorption can be observed from as early as the seventh week to as late as the twelfth week of gestation. Resorption of gestational sacs during pregnancy frequently happens without affecting the co-twin. There are excellent chances for survival of the other twin, as resorption typically occurs in the first trimester. [11]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Blighted ovum: By definition, a blighted ovum is the gestational sac inside which no embryo can be visualized via ultrasonography. According to results from some studies, most of the pregnancies that ended with a vanishing fetus were subsequently found to be an anembryonic pregnancy coexisting with a normal pregnancy. The result could be in the form of vaginal bleeding in the first trimester, indicating the expulsion of the anembryonic sac. Underging a thorough ultrasonographic examination before opting for dilation and curettage is advisable, as the process of dilation and curettage may end up in the accidental abortion of the other surviving twin. [11]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Fetus papyraceous: Fetus papyraceous is a mummified, compressed, or flattened fetus associated with another viable fetus. [12] This occurrence is very rare. The deceased fetus is flattened between the membranes of the viable fetus and the uterine wall. [13] The demise of the fetus usually occurs in the first trimester or early in the second trimester. The early demised twin is not completely resorbed. As the pregnancy continues to term, the twin may become macerated, which may affect the other viable twin. This course of events can be well observed via regular ultrasonographic examinations. [7] [14] Additionally, a vanishing twin has also been linked with several fetal malformations in the surviving twin via an unknown mechanism. [7] Fetus papyraceous occurs in 1 out of 12,000 pregnancies and 1 out of 200 twin pregnancies. [13]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Examining the placenta after delivering the viable co-twin may help to understand the morphologic characteristics of the lost twin. Although a vanished twin pregnancy can be noted via ultrasound, no such histologic confirmatory evidence has been presented previously. [15] The results of studies examining the placenta ranged from histologically normal anembryonic gestational sacs to identifiable residues of fetal tissue. [16] In some cases, a mummified, compressed fetus is present in association with a viable fetus as described above, a condition called fetus papyraceous. [14] In a study, the histopathologic examination of the placenta revealed a gestational sac containing amorphous material, surrounded by degenerated chorionic villi, adjacent to a normal amniochorionic membrane. [15] Another study's results revealed well-delineated plaques of fibrin deposits and embryonic tissue remnants, hinting at the disappearance of a conceptus. [17]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: The increased risk of VTS in pregnancies with intrauterine hematoma (IUH) may be due to several factors. These include physical damage from the hematoma, poor blood vessel development, and weak or easily damaged blood vessels. IUH might also interfere with how well the uterine lining supports embryonic implantation, disrupting communication between the embryo and the endometrium, which can lead to either threatened miscarriage or VTS. Another possible cause of IUH is bleeding from the vessels at the edge of the placenta. This bleeding can lead to early blood flow into the space between the placenta and uterus, affecting how well the placenta develops and handles oxidative stress. The resulting cell damage in the placenta can contribute to the development of VTS. Other pregnancy complications, such as preterm birth, miscarriage risk, and heavy bleeding after delivery, may also be more common after VTS. According to Zhu et al, these issues tend to be more severe in the surviving twin as compared to a singleton pregnancy. [10]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Besides being asymptomatic, the most likely clinical presentation of a vanishing twin pregnancy is vaginal bleeding or spotting, uterine cramps, or pelvic pain. These symptoms may be associated with the loss of 1 conceptus. During the first trimester of pregnancy, these symptoms also may go unnoticed by the mother.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Patients, especially those who conceived via ART, are understandably worried about the outcomes of the vanishing twin on the viable co-twin. When multiple embryos are transferred into the uterus, the chances of twin gestation and the vanishing twin phenomenon increase. [5] The history will usually indicate a previously documented fetal heart activity or more than 1 gestational sac to spontaneous reduction into a singleton pregnancy, as per subsequent ultrasonographic findings through later gestational ages or at the time of delivery. [5] [18]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: VTS is typically diagnosed through 2 ultrasounds performed at different stages of early pregnancy. The initial scan, usually around 6 to 7 weeks of gestation, reveals a multiple pregnancy, while a follow-up scan later in the first trimester shows only 1 fetus with a detectable heartbeat. [8] Examination via ultrasound during pregnancy confirms the presence of the vanishing twin phenomenon. Additionally, the examination of the placenta after giving birth provides morphological details about the vanishing twin that was established following an ultrasonographic examination. [19]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: A study performed to compare the rise of human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) between normally progressing twin pregnancies and pregnancies with vanishing twins demonstrated a slower rise of hCG in vanishing twin pregnancies as compared to the normal twin pregnancies. The reason for the slower rate of hCG rise could be due to poor trophoblastic activity resulting from embryonic causes. These findings indicate that the abnormality in the hCG in VTS is present from the earliest days of implantation and is not due to some acute insult. [20]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: A recent study, which included a large series of pregnancies with a vanishing twin, was conducted to investigate the use of maternal serum pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) and serum-free β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) in first-trimester screening for trisomies in relation to the interval between embryonic demise and blood sampling. Compared to previous studies, this study's results revealed that the multiples of the median (MoM) values of maternal serum-free β-hCG were not altered; however, those of PAPP-A (MoM) were increased in both pregnancies with an empty gestational sac or 1 nonviable embryo. [21] If the pregnancy is conceived via an ART and complicated by advanced maternal age, the chances of the vanishing twin phenomenon occurring get higher, most probably due to the increased chances of chromosomal abnormalities in the fetus associated with advanced maternal age. [22] A regular prenatal examination is highly advisable in such cases, which includes: ultrasonographic examinations and first- and second-trimester maternal serum markers. [23] [24]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: There is no specific medical care necessary for an uncomplicated vanishing twin pregnancy when the twin is lost during the first trimester. The other fetus has a high chance of survival and is frequently delivered without incident. [25] On the other hand, if the disappearance of a twin complicates the pregnancy during the second or third trimester, then the pregnancy could be treated as a high-risk pregnancy, as the outcomes of such pregnancies might affect the other twin adversely. Regular prenatal visits to assess any signs of complications and to keep a check on both maternal and fetal health are necessary to avoid adverse outcomes for both mother and fetus. [5]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: A global survey of affected patients found that most patients affected by VTS had a negative experience with their caregiver. More than 40% of patients reported not receiving education about the chorionicity of the condition or its significance, despite its impact on pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, there were differences in management across various countries. [2]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Careful ultrasonographic assessment is required to diagnose a vanishing twin in early pregnancy, as any artifact may incorrectly indicate the presence of an additional gestational sac, or any pathology of the placenta, such as placental cysts, may incorrectly imply multiple gestations. Histologic examination of the placenta by the experts after delivery is necessary in such cases. [3]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Data on the accuracy of noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for trisomy 13, 18, and 21 have been limited in both twin pregnancies and pregnancies affected by VTS. Fetal DNA from the vanishing twin may be present in maternal blood up to 8 weeks after the demise, and potentially up to 15 weeks later. Since chromosomal abnormalities are a common underlying cause of miscarriage, when a vanishing twin is present, trisomies may contribute to elevated rates of false-positive screening results when using cell-free DNA (cfDNA) aneuploidy testing.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: A recent study published in the Journal of Human Genetics reported that NIPT was useful in pregnancies with a vanishing twin, with no false-negative tests occurring. Use of NIPT in twin pregnancies, especially those affected by VTS, may be reassuring to the mother. [26] Another study performed in France found that NIPT effectively screens for trisomy 21 in vanishing twin pregnancies, but may not be as accurate for trisomy 18 and 13, as the fetal fraction is low due to the presence of less placental tissue. [27] Individual fetal fractions can be measured in dizygotic pregnancies to ensure that both results are satisfactory. Given this, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the Society for Maternal–Fetal Medicine (SMFM) advise offering diagnostic testing in multifetal pregnancies where a vanishing twin is detected, as serum-based aneuploidy screening or cfDNA testing may yield misleading results. [1]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management
content: There is conflicting data on the outcomes of pregnancies complicated by VTS. In a retrospective cohort study of over 1000 frozen embryo transfer pregnancies affected by VTS, which resulted in a single live newborn, the risk ratios of preterm birth and low birth weight in these pregnancies as compared to singleton pregnancies were 1.53 and 1.76, respectively. Gestational age at birth was earlier in the affected pregnancies as well. [28] Iatrogenic and spontaneous preterm birth and fetal growth abnormalities later in pregnancy have been associated with the surviving twin in a pregnancy that has been affected by a vanishing twin. [27] [29] Further studies are needed to delineate these and other possible correlations. Pregnancies affected by VTS have also been associated with very low birth weight and low Apgar scores. [30]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: The chances of survival of the viable co-twin are excellent if the demise of the twin occurs during the first trimester of pregnancy. The health of the mother is not affected, except for some mild vaginal bleeding that may be experienced as a sign of the loss of the embryo in early pregnancy. In other words, the earlier the loss of the fetus, the more likely it is that the mother may not notice the twin being lost, as chances of survival of the other fetus and the health of the mother may not be affected by the loss of the fetus. [25] [31]

The health of the mother is not affected, except for some mild vaginal bleeding that may be experienced as a sign of the loss of the embryo in early pregnancy. In other words, the earlier the loss of the fetus, the more likely it is that the mother may not notice the twin being lost, as chances of survival of the other fetus and the health of the mother may not be affected by the loss of the fetus. [25] [31]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Complications
content: As noted above, if the fetus is lost during the first trimester of pregnancy, ie, in the embryonic stage, the mother is most likely to experience the complication of the vanishing twin in the form of vaginal bleeding or spotting, pelvic cramps, or back pain. However, many individuals are asymptomatic. The chances of survival of the viable co-twin are good in such cases. [32] On the other hand, the chances of complications are higher in the existing co-twin if the demise of the twin occurs later in gestation. Complications may include cerebral palsy of the viable twin, intrauterine growth restriction of the viable twin, premature labor, and other congenital anomalies accompanied by a fetus papyraceous. [7]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Complications
content: A study was performed recently among singleton pregnancies, twin pregnancies, and women with vanishing twin pregnancies. The study's results revealed adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes among vanishing twin pregnancies compared to the other 2 groups. Among maternal complications, gestational diabetes, premature rupture of membranes, oligohydramnios, cervical insufficiency, labor induction, and preterm labor were higher in vanishing twin pregnancies than in singleton and twin pregnancies. [33]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Complications
content: Among neonatal outcomes, fetal malformations were recorded more often in vanishing twin pregnancies than in singleton and twin pregnancies. [33] Although cerebral palsy has no specific etiology, it is accepted through consensus that the death of a twin in late gestation is associated with higher chances of the surviving twin having cerebral palsy. [31] Pregnancies diagnosed with the VTS after IVF, compared with those that were spontaneously conceived, carried a higher rate of obstetric complications with regard to preterm deliveries, gestational diabetes, placental insertion abnormalities, and low birth weight. [34] [35]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Complications
content: Having regular prenatal follow-up and the pregnancy assessed with the help of ultrasonographic examinations is advisable for obtaining knowledge about fetal anomalies associated with the demise of the twin. However, most vanishing twin pregnancies will remain uncomplicated throughout gestation and birth. Study results show that the birth weight was found to be slightly lower in the co-twin in a vanishing twin pregnancy as compared to a nonvanishing twin pregnancy. [32] Caution should be taken when interpreting data showing adverse outcomes in the surviving twin, as this may be due to publication bias. More robust studies are needed to clarify the association between VTS and adverse outcomes in the surviving twin, in order to draw conclusions with greater certainty. [5]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Complications
content: VTS usually happens early in pregnancy, often before the first trimester screening. As a result, it can impact the accuracy of blood tests that screen for conditions such as Down syndrome. If clinicians don't know a twin was lost, they might misinterpret the results and think the remaining baby has a medical condition, even if they are healthy. Even when VTS is known, the accuracy of the test can still drop because the blood tests are not adjusted for this situation. This effect is because DNA from the lost twin stays in the mother's blood for many weeks and can confuse the results of NIPT. Studies have investigated the potential impact of VTS on results from first- and second-trimester blood tests. Some study results found specific markers, such as PAPP-A and Inhibin A, to be increased, but the results were not consistent across all studies. For example, 5 studies' results showed no change in β-hCG levels, and 1 study's showed an increase. Results from 2 studies on another marker, uE3, both found no change. [36]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Although most pregnancies associated with a vanishing twin will be without complications, it is, however, necessary to relieve the anxiety of the parents regarding the outcomes of the pregnancy and the health of the twin whose co-twin was lost. Routine prenatal follow-up throughout the gestation is advisable to monitor the health of the surviving twin. No specific medical care is necessary if the co-twin was lost during the first trimester of pregnancy.

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: The chances of survival of the co-twin are excellent if the co-twin is lost during the first trimester, and the health of the mother and the baby is most likely not affected. If the twin is lost during the second or third trimester, the survival of the co-twin is at risk, and there are higher chances of fetal malformations and anomalies in the surviving twin, for example, cerebral palsy. [31] [33] All information regarding the etiological factors associated with a vanishing twin pregnancy and the possible outcomes must be provided to the patient. [4] [25]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: NIPT with cfDNA in twin pregnancies can be offered and is endorsed by American College of Obstetriciand and Gynecologists and the International Society for Prenatal Diagnosis. [27]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: VTS is the spontaneous loss of 1 fetus in a multiple pregnancy, usually in the first trimester, with partial or complete resorption. Some definitions require prior documentation of cardiac activity in all fetuses before the loss. [1] A complicated vanishing twin pregnancy carries risks of premature labor, obstructed labor, intrauterine growth restriction of the surviving fetus, neurodevelopmental impairment, placental abruption that may cause the death of the surviving fetus, and chorioamnionitis. [4] Care coordination among healthcare team members, including obstetricians/gynecologists, nurses, and clinical staff, is essential before and during pregnancy. Detecting a vanishing twin during early pregnancy via ultrasonographic examination has many benefits. If the loss of a twin is identified during the second or third trimester, the clinician needs to monitor more carefully the health of the mother and the remaining fetus and watch closely for any complications. [4] An interprofessional approach to patient healthcare is necessary to prevent errors and improve clinical outcomes through effective communication, staying current on the patient’s current health status, recent physical and diagnostic evaluations, and mental well-being. [37]

title: Vanishing Twin Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Substantial deficiencies exist in how clinicians communicate with patients and in varying approaches to managing VTS. Many patients report inadequate explanations, absent emotional support, and inconsistent handling of clinical details. Bridging these gaps requires enhanced provider training, clearer care pathways, and the adoption of standardized protocols. Focusing on patient-centered communication, early assessment of chorionicity, and providing evidence-based guidance could significantly enhance the patient experience and decision-making process. Looking ahead, research should investigate the effectiveness of training programs and structured interventions aimed at improving clinical practice in VTS and related losses. Specific emphasis should be given to developing guidelines that incorporate bereavement care, screening intricacies (such as lingering cfDNA or placental sequelae), and tailored emotional support strategies across pregnancy and postpartum contexts. [2]
